This is the first module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd), and it is written for the person who arrives with no R at all: a student, a professional from another field, or anyone curious about how the analysis of the course is built. It does not assume that you have programmed before. Sections 1 to 13 work on one file, the housing-audit data, which holds one row for each of the 1,014 emails that the original authors (OAs) sent to public housing authorities in the United States, signed with names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic applicant [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]. The [case study](../cases/housing/index.qmd) tells the story of the experiment. Here it serves as a dataset small enough to look at whole, with an outcome that is either yes or no, which makes it a good place to learn. By the end you will be able to read the file into R, look at it, reshape it with a handful of verbs, compute the share of replies that greeted the sender by name and the difference between two such shares, set the result out as a table and as a figure, and fit your first specification with the helper that the exercise uses.

Sections 14 to 18 take the same tools further, for a second reading. Section 14 reads the Stata file that the OAs deposited, with its labels, and introduces the packages that fetch data from an archive. Section 15 sets out the three dialects in which R is written, section 16 the grammar of graphics in more depth, section 17 the specification curve, and section 18 the habit of naming the estimand before a model is read. Sections 14, 15 and 18 stay with the emails. Sections 16 and 17 move to the country-year panel of the EU-frames case, a table of 270 rows built from Eurobarometer surveys, for two things that the emails cannot show. A scatterplot with a fitted line needs measures that vary continuously, and the panel holds them, among them the unemployment rate and the mean score with which the respondents of a country-year framed the EU in cosmopolitan terms. The curve of that case mixes predictors whose results point in opposite directions, so it has to be aligned with the claim before it can be read.

Unlike many pages that teach R, this one runs its code. Every block in sections 1 to 15 and in section 18 was executed when the page was built, and what R printed appears underneath it, so you can compare your own output with the page line by line. The code of sections 16 and 17 is shown without being run, because it reads the panel of the EU-frames case, which is on your machine once you have the workspace of that case. The way to learn is still to type. Copy each block into the workspace that you downloaded from the [setup page](../setup.qmd), or into the [browser lab](../cases/housing/lab.qmd), where a copy of R starts inside the browser tab with the data already in place.

The courses use the module at several points. It is the companion of the R tutorial in Part 2 of the [one-day course on data tools](../tracks/housing-one-day-data-tools/part-2.qmd), which works on the same emails, and of the first session of day 2 in the three-day courses, for example on the [immigration-and-trust case](../tracks/trust-three-days/day-2.qmd). The self-study track reads sections 1 to 5 in [stage 1](../tracks/self-study/stage-1.qmd) and sections 6 to 13 in [stage 2](../tracks/self-study/stage-2.qmd).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

The browser lab is the quickest way to follow along on a first read, since there is nothing to install. It loads the data for you as an object called `audit` and has datawizard, dplyr, tinyplot and parameters ready, but it does not hold readr, tinytable, ggplot2, haven, performance or modelbased. Skip the line that reads the file in [section 6](#sec-reading), the formatted table in [section 11](#sec-table), the ggplot2 figures at the end of [section 12](#sec-ggplot), the Stata file of [section 14](#sec-formats) and everything in [section 18](#sec-easystats) after `parameters::model_parameters()`; everything else runs there as printed.
:::

## 1. R and the IDE {#sec-what}

**R** is a programming language built for working with data: reading it, reshaping it, fitting statistical models to it and drawing figures from it. It is free and open source, and it is one of the common languages of quantitative social science, which is why the analysis of the course is written in it. On its own, R is a program that reads instructions and returns answers.

**The IDE** is the program from which you drive R. An IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.), short for integrated development environment, is a window with your files on one side, a place to write and run code, and panels that show results, figures and the objects you have made. Newcomers often run the language and the environment together, although each is installed separately. You install R once, so that the language is on your machine, and you install an IDE once, as the place where you work. When the IDE first opens, it finds the R that you installed and connects to it. The [setup page](../setup.qmd) walks through both installations, and the [IDE module](ide.qmd) sets the three common IDEs side by side, pane by pane.

## 2. The console, the script and the report {#sec-surfaces}

There are three surfaces into which you type R, and knowing which is for what saves a great deal of confusion later.

The **console** is the interactive prompt. You type one line, press Enter, and R answers immediately. It is the place to try something out, check a value or do a quick sum. Its weakness is that everything typed there is lost when the session closes, with no record of how you reached a result.

A **script** is a plain text file with the extension `.R` that holds a sequence of commands you want to keep. You write the commands in the script and send them to the console from there, all at once or line by line. A script runs the same way tomorrow and on someone else's machine, and it shows step by step how a result was produced. The course follows a simple rule: try things in the console, and move anything that matters into a script.

A **Quarto document**, with the extension `.qmd`, is a script and a written report in one file. It holds ordinary prose with blocks of R code, called chunks, between the paragraphs. When the document is rendered, R runs every chunk and places its results, whether tables, figures or numbers, into the finished report at the point where they belong. The workspace of the course holds the same exercise in both forms: `working_script.R` takes you through Tasks 1 to 5 as a plain script, and `index.qmd` is the report that you fill in and render. The [Quarto module](quarto.qmd) shows how such a document is written.

## 3. Objects and vectors {#sec-objects}

R works by putting values into named **objects** and then referring to them by name. You assign a value to a name with the arrow `<-`, typed as a less-than sign followed by a hyphen. From then on, the name stands in for the value.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
emails_sent <- 1014         # a single number
first_name  <- "Santiago"   # text, called a character string, is quoted
bounced     <- FALSE        # a logical value: TRUE or FALSE

emails_sent                 # typing a name prints its value
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1014
```


:::
:::


Most data come as runs of values rather than single ones. A **vector** is an ordered run of values of one type, built with `c()`, for 'combine'. Arithmetic works on the whole vector at once, which is why R rarely needs the loops that other languages reach for. The two vectors below hold, for the white, the Black and the Hispanic names in turn, the number of emails that reached an official and the number of replies that came back.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
delivered <- c(308, 326, 357)   # white, Black and Hispanic names
replies   <- c(177, 198, 188)

replies / delivered             # three reply rates, in one step
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.5746753 0.6073620 0.5266106
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
sum(replies)                    # every reply
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 563
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
replies[3]                      # the third value: the Hispanic names
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 188
```


:::
:::


These six numbers were typed by hand, and [section 9](#sec-verbs) computes them from the file, which is how you would check them.

One small fact carries most of the arithmetic of the course. When a vector holds only 1s and 0s, its **mean is the share of 1s**. The outcome of the claim, whether a reply opened with the name of the sender, is stored in exactly that way, with 1 for a greeting by name and 0 for none, so the share of replies that greeted the sender by name is the mean of that column.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
greeted <- c(1, 0, 1, 1, 0)   # five replies: 1 = opened with the name of the sender
mean(greeted)                 # three of the five
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.6
```


:::
:::


Real data also have gaps. R marks a missing value with `NA`, for 'not available', and any calculation that meets one returns `NA` in turn, because the answer cannot be known. The argument `na.rm = TRUE` tells a summary function to remove the missing values first.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
greeted <- c(1, 0, NA, 1, 0)   # the third reply carries no greeting code
mean(greeted)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] NA
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
mean(greeted, na.rm = TRUE)    # the share among the four coded replies
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.5
```


:::
:::


The housing-audit data have missing values of three kinds, and each means something different: an email that bounced has no reply status, an email without a reply has no greeting, and 5 replies were never coded for their greeting. Deciding what to do with each of them is part of the analysis, which is why the course never uses `na.rm = TRUE` without saying which rows it removes.

## 4. Data frames {#sec-dataframes}

A **data frame** is how R stores a table: a set of vectors of equal length standing side by side as columns, with one row per observation. Almost everything in the course is a data frame. Here is a small one built by hand, three emails with the name that signed each, whether a reply came, and whether the reply greeted the sender by name:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
emails <- data.frame(
  name  = c("Brett", "Santiago", "Emily"),
  reply = c(1, 1, 0),
  named = c(1, 0, NA)
)

emails
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
      name reply named
1    Brett     1     1
2 Santiago     1     0
3    Emily     0    NA
```


:::
:::


Base R, the core that ships with R itself, reaches into a data frame with two operators. The `$` sign pulls out one column as a vector, and square brackets take a block by `[rows, columns]`, where an empty slot means 'all of them'.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
emails$named   # one column, as a vector
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1]  1  0 NA
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
emails[1:2, ]  # the first two rows, every column
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
      name reply named
1    Brett     1     1
2 Santiago     1     0
```


:::
:::


You will meet both in code that other people write, and `$` is often the quickest way to look at a single column. For reshaping a table, the course uses the verbs of [section 9](#sec-verbs), which say in words what each step does. The emails without a reply show why the third value of `named` is missing: no reply, so no greeting to code.

## 5. Packages {#sec-packages}

Everything so far, from `c()` to `mean()` and `data.frame()`, comes with R itself. Everything else arrives as **packages**: bundles of functions and their documentation, written by researchers and developers and published on CRAN, the Comprehensive R Archive Network, which holds more than twenty thousand of them. The function that reads a CSV file in the next section, `read_csv()`, comes from a package called readr, and the sections after it lean on packages for nearly everything.

Using a package takes two steps, and the difference between them trips nearly every newcomer at least once. The block below is shown and not run, because installing is something that you do once on your own machine.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
install.packages("pak")   # once on a new machine: the installer of the course # r-style: keep – the one-off bootstrap of pak
pak::pak("readr")         # step 1: download a package to your machine – once
readr::read_csv("data/housing_audit.csv")   # step 2: call a function by its package and its name
```
:::


`pak::pak()` downloads a package, together with everything that it depends on, and stores it on your machine. You run it once, and again only when you want an update. The second step is the call itself, and the course writes every function that does not come with R by the name of its package, two colons and the name of the function, as in `readr::read_csv()`. Written that way, a line works in any session on a machine where the package is installed, and anyone who reads it can see at once where each function comes from, which matters when two packages offer functions of the same name. You will also meet the older habit of attaching a package to the session with `library(readr)` at the top of a script, after which its functions can be called by their names alone. The two error messages that you will meet most often come from these two steps: `there is no package called 'readr'` means that step 1 never happened on this machine, and `could not find function "read_csv"` means that the function was called by its name alone in a session to which its package was never attached.

Research code that only its authors run, such as the scripts of a paper, is often written the other way, with every function called by its name alone, and the facilitator of the course writes it so. What keeps it readable is a single import script, run at the top of every other script of the project, that attaches each package with `library()` and lists in `include.only` the functions that the project takes from it. Anyone who wants to know where a function comes from then has one place to look. Two attached packages can offer functions of the same name, and the conflicted package stops with an error when such a name is called, until `conflicts_prefer()` has said which of the two is meant:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# R/00_packages.R: the packages of a project and the functions taken from each
library(readr, include.only = c("read_csv", "write_csv"))
library(datawizard, include.only = c("data_filter", "data_summary", "data_tabulate"))
library(dplyr, include.only = c("filter", "if_else"))
library(conflicted)
conflicts_prefer(dplyr::filter)   # stats::filter(), which R attaches at start-up, has the same name
```
:::


The course writes `pkg::fun()` in all of its own code because that code is read a block at a time, by people who did not write it, and each block has to say where its functions come from without an import script beside it.

In the workspace, `R/check_setup.R` checks the twelve packages that the exercise needs (dplyr, purrr, readr, tibble, datawizard, parameters, sandwich, marginaleffects, effectsize, tinyplot, dagitty and rmarkdown) and, if any are missing, prints the line that installs them.

## 6. Reading the data {#sec-reading}

You will rarely type data by hand. Most data arrive as a **CSV** file, short for 'comma-separated values': a plain text table in which each line is a row and commas divide the columns. The course ships its data this way because any program can open a CSV, and because version control can compare two versions of it line by line. `read_csv()` from readr reads one into a data frame:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
audit <- readr::read_csv("data/housing_audit.csv")
```

A relative path works on any machine that holds the project, and an absolute path breaks as soon as the work moves. Open the workspace folder in your IDE, and every path in the course works as written.

## 8. The pipe {#sec-pipe}

Most of the work after reading data is reshaping it, and reshaping is almost always a sequence of steps. The **pipe**, written `|>`, exists to make such sequences readable. It takes whatever stands on its left and passes it as the first argument to the function on its right, so that instead of wrapping functions inside one another and reading them from the inside out, you write the steps from top to bottom in the order in which they happen:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# without the pipe: read from the innermost function outwards
round(mean(audit$reply, na.rm = TRUE), 3) # r-style: keep – shown for comparison
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.568
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# with the pipe: read from left to right, in the order of the steps
audit$reply |> mean(na.rm = TRUE) |> round(3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.568
```


:::
:::


Both lines give the share of delivered emails that drew a reply. On one short line the gain is small, but it grows with every step of the chains in the next section, which is why nearly all modern R is written this way. You will also meet an older pipe, `%>%`, from a package called magrittr, in code written before 2021, when the native `|>` became part of R. Read the two in the same way, and write `|>`, as all the materials of the course do.

## 9. The datawizard verbs {#sec-verbs}

The datawizard package, one of the easystats packages of [section 15](#sec-dialects), gives each common operation on a table a named verb. Each takes a data frame as its first argument and returns a data frame, which is what lets the verbs be chained with the pipe:

- `data_filter()` keeps the rows that meet a condition;
- `data_select()` keeps the columns that you name;
- `data_modify()` adds a column or changes one;
- `data_summary()` collapses many rows into one row of summaries, and with `by` into one row per group;
- `data_tabulate()` counts rows, as section 7 showed.

The dplyr package of the tidyverse has a verb for each of these, `filter()`, `select()`, `mutate()`, `summarise()` and `count()`, and you will meet them in code written by others and in a few places in the code of the course, where datawizard has no verb for the job. The course uses datawizard first, so that one family of packages covers the data work and the reading of models.

## 10. A share and a difference in shares {#sec-shares}

The claim of the case is that replies to emails signed with Hispanic names were less likely to greet the sender by name than replies to emails signed with white names. In the terms of [section 3](#sec-objects), that is a comparison of two means of a 0/1 column, so you already have the tools for it. Keep the replies that carry a greeting code, keep the white and the Hispanic names, and summarise the column `named` in each group:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
shares <- audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named), group %in% c("white", "hispanic")) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(
    replies = n(),
    greeted = sum(named),
    share   = mean(named),
    by = "group"
  )

shares
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

------------------------------------
hispanic |     187 |      77 |  0.41
white    |     175 |     107 |  0.61
```


:::
:::


61.1% of the replies to white names opened with the name of the sender, against 41.2% of the replies to Hispanic names. The difference between the two shares is the estimate that the course starts from. Inside `data_summary()`, square brackets pick out the value of one group, and multiplying by 100 turns a difference in shares into a difference in percentage points:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
shares |>
  datawizard::data_summary(gap_points = 100 * (share[group == "hispanic"] - share[group == "white"]))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
gap_points
----------
    -19.97
```


:::
:::


A gap of −19.97 points is the raw difference that the paper reports, and it is the **reference specification** of the course, the analysis against which every alternative on the [specification menu](../cases/housing/menu.qmd) is compared. The published estimate of −20.0 points comes from a different calculation, a logistic regression with covariates, which the [binary-outcomes module](binary-outcomes.qmd) fits step by step, and the two agree closely.

That gap is counted among the replies only. An email that drew no reply has no greeting, so it plays no part in the calculation. The other way to count is to keep every delivered email and treat a missing reply as a reply without a greeting by name. `if_else()` from dplyr makes that column inside `data_modify()`: where `reply` is 1 it keeps the greeting code, and elsewhere it puts 0. The five uncoded replies are still missing afterwards and are filtered out.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply), group %in% c("white", "hispanic")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(greeted = dplyr::if_else(reply == 1, named, 0)) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(greeted)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(emails = n(), share = mean(greeted), by = "group")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

-------------------------
hispanic |    356 |  0.22
white    |    306 |  0.35
```


:::
:::


Counted this way, the gap is −13.34 points. The two numbers answer two questions. Among the replies, the comparison asks whether officials who answered wrote differently to the two groups of names. Among all delivered emails, it asks whether the name changed the chance of receiving a reply that greeted the sender by name at all, which mixes the decision to reply with the tone of the reply. Which emails are counted is the second argument of `try_spec()` in Task 4, and of all the decisions on the menu it is the one that moves the estimate furthest. The [causal-graphs module](dags.qmd#sec-collider) explains why the comparison among replies needs care, and the [audit-experiments module](experiments.qmd#sec-posttreatment) works through what each comparison assumes.

## 11. A first table {#sec-table}

A summary built with datawizard is already a table, and printing it in the console is enough while you work. For a report, the numbers need readable column names, sensible rounding and a caption. The chain below builds one row per group of names with the five counts that the case rests on and two percentages:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
by_group <- audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply)) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(
    delivered = n(),
    replies   = sum(reply),
    coded     = sum(!is.na(named)),
    greeted   = sum(named, na.rm = TRUE),
    by = "group"
  ) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(
    reply_pct   = 100 * replies / delivered,
    greeted_pct = 100 * greeted / coded
  ) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("-greeted_pct")

by_group
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------

hispanic |       357 |     188 |   187 |      77 |     52.66 |       41.18
```

### tinyplot {#sec-tinyplot}

tinyplot extends the graphics system that comes with R itself and needs no other package, which is why it is light enough to run in the browser lab [@McDermottEtAl2026TinyplotLightweightExtension]. A plot is one call with two parts: a **formula** with the data, which says what goes on which axis, and a **type**, which says what to draw.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tinyplot::tinyplot(share ~ name, data = by_name, type = "p", flip = TRUE)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![The share of replies that greeted the sender by name, by name: the first draft with tinyplot.](intro-r_files/figure-html/fig-tinyplot-first-1.png){#fig-tinyplot-first width=672}
:::
:::


The formula `share ~ name` is read 'share by name', as in a model formula: the column before the tilde goes on the vertical axis and the column after it on the horizontal one. `type = "p"` draws points, and `flip = TRUE` turns the chart on its side, so that the names are read down the vertical axis. The default look writes the labels of that axis along it, so that only some of the names fit, and the theme of the next figure sets them upright. Other types draw other marks, among them `"l"` for lines, `"s"` for the steps of a life table, `"barplot"` for bars and `"boxplot"` for boxes.

Three changes make the figure readable. A vertical bar in the formula, `share ~ name | group`, colours each mark by a third column and adds a legend that explains the colours. `type = "barplot"` draws one bar per row, with a length equal to the value in the data. And `reorder(name, share)`, applied to the data before the plot, sorts the names by the value being plotted rather than alphabetically.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
by_name_sorted <- by_name |>
  datawizard::data_modify(name  = reorder(name, share),
                          group = factor(group, levels = c("white", "black", "hispanic"),
                                         labels = c("white", "Black", "Hispanic")))

tinyplot::tinytheme("minimal")
tinyplot::tinyplot(share ~ name | group, data = by_name_sorted, type = "barplot", flip = TRUE,
                   palette = c("grey60", "#4a78ab", "#8b1538"),
                   legend = list(title = "Names meant to indicate"),
                   xlab = NA, ylab = "Replies that greeted the sender by name (%)")
tinyplot::tinytheme()
```

`palette` gives one colour for each group, in the order of the levels of the factor, which is why the groups are made a factor first, with the labels that the legend should show. `legend` sets the title of the legend. `xlab` and `ylab` supply the words on the axes; with `flip = TRUE`, `xlab` still belongs to the column after the tilde, now drawn vertically, and `NA` leaves it blank. `tinytheme("minimal")` sets the look of everything that carries no data, the gridlines, the frame and the type, until `tinytheme()` without an argument restores the default.

A third column can also split a figure into panels with shared axes, which are called **facets**. The chart below compares the female and the male names of each group, with `facet = ~name_sex`. Make the column of the facets a factor first, so that each panel is headed by its label:

### ggplot2 {#sec-first-ggplot}

The ggplot2 package draws the figures of the pages and slides of this site. Its name abbreviates 'the grammar of graphics', the idea that any chart can be described as a combination of a few standard parts: the data, a mapping from columns to visual properties such as position and colour, and the shapes that are drawn, called geoms. Scales, labels and a theme finish the figure. A bar chart and a scatterplot are two fillings of the same parts, so once you know the parts you can read the code of any figure on this site.

A plot needs data, a mapping and at least one geom, and everything else has a default good enough to start with:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot2::ggplot(by_name, ggplot2::aes(x = share, y = name)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![The share of replies that greeted the sender by name, by name: the first draft.](intro-r_files/figure-html/fig-first-1.png){#fig-first width=672}
:::
:::


`ggplot()` receives the data frame. `aes()` is the **aesthetic mapping**, which says that the share governs the horizontal position and the name the vertical position. `geom_col()` draws one bar per row, with a length equal to the value in the data. Its cousin `geom_bar()` counts the rows for you instead, and reaching for the wrong one of the two is a frequent small frustration. Layers are joined with `+`, never with the pipe: ggplot2 settled on `+` years before R had a native pipe, and typing `|>` where `+` belongs is among the commonest errors of the first week.

The bars come out in alphabetical order and in one colour. The same two changes make the figure readable. `reorder(name, share)` sorts the names by the value being plotted, and `fill = group` inside `aes()` **maps** the colour of each bar to the group of its name, so that ggplot2 adds a legend explaining the colours. A property given outside `aes()`, such as `fill = "#0e3b6a"` in `geom_col()`, is **set** instead: one fixed value for every bar, with no legend because there is nothing to explain.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot2::ggplot(by_name, ggplot2::aes(x = share, y = reorder(name, share), fill = group)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(white = "grey60", black = "#4a78ab", hispanic = "#8b1538"),
    labels = c(white = "white", black = "Black", hispanic = "Hispanic"),
    name   = "Names meant to indicate"
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Replies that greeted the sender by name (%)", y = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

The **scale** decides which colours the mapping uses. `scale_fill_manual()` names a colour for each group, and giving `values` and `labels` as named vectors, with `white = …` rather than a bare list of colours, means that the assignment cannot reverse itself if the groups arrive in another order. `labs()` supplies the words, which deserve more care than beginners give them, because a column name such as `share` means nothing to a reader who has not opened the codebook. `theme_minimal()` sets the look of everything that carries no data, and its `base_size` scales all the type at once.

Read the figure as the claim of the case. Both Hispanic names drew fewer greetings by name than any other name, and the two names that were meant to indicate each group do not always agree, which is why the design used a male and a female name for every group. Unlike a tinyplot, a ggplot2 plot is an ordinary R object, so it can be stored under a name and written to a file with `ggplot2::ggsave("names.png", p, width = 7, height = 4)`, which takes its dimensions in inches.

::: {.callout-tip}

```r
emails <- arrow::read_parquet("housing_audit.parquet")   # arrow::read_feather() for Feather
```

Whatever the source format, what you end up with in R is the same data frame, and everything downstream – the verbs of sections 8 and 9, the models fitted in later modules – proceeds identically. Every `read_` function here also has a `write_` counterpart (`write_csv()`, `write_dta()`, `write_parquet()`, and `write_xlsx()` from the `writexl` package), so R also serves as the converter between all of these formats. The course ships its data as CSV all the same, because for tables of a few hundred or a thousand rows the efficiency of the binary formats buys nothing, while plain text can be opened in anything, compared line by line or read in an email.

### Fetching data from a repository or an API {#sec-fetching}

Most data come from an archive, a statistical office or a repository, and for many of those sources an R package fetches the data straight into a data frame. The query is then written down in your script instead of being clicked through on a website, and that is what makes the download repeatable. The [data sources module](data-sources.qmd) maps the sources and works through the route of each case of the course step by step, while this subsection covers the packages that query them, which fall into three groups.

**Repositories of deposited work**, which need no account for a public file. The `dataverse` package downloads a file from any Dataverse installation by the DOI of its record, which is how the [data sources module](data-sources.qmd#sec-dataverse) fetches the deposited file that this section read:

```r
deposit <- dataverse::get_dataframe_by_name(
  "HousingAuditAJPSFinalPublic_Unidentified.tab",
  dataset  = "doi:10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU",
  server   = "dataverse.harvard.edu",
  original = TRUE,             # the Stata file as deposited, not the tab-separated copy
  .f       = haven::read_dta   # the function that reads it
)
```

`osfr` reads and writes the Open Science Framework through its API, which is how the script `R/get_data.R` in the workspace of the EU-frames case fetches its panel, and `zen4R` does the same for Zenodo, and deposits there as well. For a source with no package, `httr2` sends the request and `jsonlite` parses the answer, and `rvest` reads a table out of a web page, with the caution that scraping a site is subject to its terms and to the courtesy of not hammering it.

**Indicators from the international organisations and statistical offices**, which are open and need no account. The `WDI` package (and `wbstats`, which covers more of the World Bank databases) queries the World Bank indicators by their codes, which is how the macro variables of the EU-frames panel were obtained, as [section 3.5](data-sources.qmd#sec-worldbank) of the data sources module sets out:

```r
macro <- WDI::WDI(country = c("DE", "FR", "GB"),
                  indicator = c(unemp = "SL.UEM.TOTL.NE.ZS", growth = "NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG"),
                  start = 2004, end = 2013)
```

The `eurostat` package does the same for the Eurostat tables (`get_eurostat("une_rt_a")` fetches the annual unemployment table, with `restatapi` as an alternative that uses the newer API, the interface through which programs request data from Eurostat); `OECD` and the general-purpose `rsdmx` query the OECD and any other service that publishes in SDMX, the standard format in which many statistical agencies exchange data; `Rilostat` reaches ILOSTAT; `onsr` the Office for National Statistics; `wid` the World Inequality Database. Each returns a long, tidy table, one row per country and period, that pivots into whatever shape a model needs.

**Survey and census microdata behind a registration.** Packages are fewer here, and less dependable, because an archive that asks for an account and a statement of purpose seldom offers programs a way in. Where one does, the credentials belong in an environment variable or a keyring, never in the script. `ipumsr` builds and downloads IPUMS extracts through the IPUMS API and reads them with their labels. The ESS Data Portal has a download API of its own, still in beta, which the data sources module calls with base R in [section 3.3](data-sources.qmd#sec-ess), because the `essurvey` package was written for the download site that the ESS replaced on 30 May 2022 and has had no release since. The GESIS archive, which distributes the Eurobarometer waves behind the EU-frames case, offers no such interface. The `gesisdata` package scripts the clicks of a download by driving a web browser, but it has not been updated since July 2023, and a report of a failed download, opened on its issue tracker in February 2025, has had no answer. The course therefore downloads the waves by hand, as [section 3.4](data-sources.qmd#sec-gesis) of the same module shows step by step. `rdhs` serves the Demographic and Health Surveys, `pewdata` the files of the Pew Research Center, and `manifestoR` the coded programmes of the Manifesto Project with an API key, and any such package is worth testing on one file before a project is built on it. Whatever the package, the file that arrives is usually Stata or SPSS, and haven reads it with its labels, as the first part of this section showed.

Two habits keep a fetched dataset reproducible. Write the fetch as a function or a script of its own, save what it returns as a dated file, and read that file in the analysis, so that the analysis does not depend on the network being up or the source being unchanged. And record the version or the download date in the file name or the README, because the World Bank and Eurostat revise past years without renaming the series.

## 15. Three dialects {#sec-dialects}

R is old enough to have grown dialects, families of packages with their own vocabulary and style, all doing the same underlying work. You will meet three – base R, the tidyverse and easystats – and this section sets the same small task in each, so that none of them ever looks foreign. The task is to keep the delivered emails, the ones with a reply status, with four of their columns.

**Base R** does it with the bracket-and-`$` machinery of [section 4](#sec-dataframes), no packages required:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
delivered <- audit[!is.na(audit$reply), c("name", "group", "reply", "named")]  # r-style: keep – base R, shown for comparison
nrow(delivered)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 991
```


:::
:::


It works, and code written this way twenty years ago still runs. Its weakness is that the brackets spell out the mechanics of the selection, so the reader must decode positions and conditions to reconstruct what the line is for.

**The tidyverse** is the dominant modern dialect, a family of packages that share one design philosophy and can be installed and attached under the single name `tidyverse` [@WickhamEtAl2019WelcomeTidyverse]. You have already met two of its members, readr, whose `read_csv()` section 6 used, and dplyr, whose `if_else()` and `transmute()` sections 10 and 11 used. In dplyr, the same task reads as a list of named steps:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
delivered <- audit |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(reply)) |>            # the delivered emails only
  dplyr::select(name, group, reply, named)   # the columns of interest
nrow(delivered)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 991
```


:::
:::


`dplyr::mutate()` derives a new column from existing ones, and `dplyr::summarise()` reduces the table to a single row, or, after `dplyr::group_by()`, to one row per group. The chain below keeps the delivered emails, adds the greeting counted among all of them, as the second calculation of [section 10](#sec-shares) did, groups the emails by the group of the name, and reports three numbers for each group:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
audit |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(reply)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(greeted = dplyr::if_else(reply == 1, named, 0)) |>   # no reply counts as no greeting
  dplyr::group_by(group) |>                                         # one set of rows per group of names
  dplyr::summarise(
    emails     = dplyr::n(),                    # how many delivered emails
    reply_rate = mean(reply),                   # the share that drew a reply
    greeted    = mean(greeted, na.rm = TRUE)    # the share greeted by name, the five uncoded replies left out
  )
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

  <chr>     <int>      <dbl>   <dbl>
1 black       326      0.607   0.340
```

Read the chain aloud and it is almost English: take the emails, keep the delivered ones, add a column for the greeting, group by the names, and for each group report the count and two shares. Readability of that kind serves reproducibility, because a reviewer who can read the code can check it, and that is why the scripts of the course are built from chains of named verbs.

**easystats** is the third dialect, and the one that the course reaches for first. It is likewise a family of packages under one installable name, `easystats` [@LudeckeEtAl2022EasystatsFrameworkEasy]. ## 16. The grammar of graphics {#sec-grammar}

[Section 12](#sec-ggplot) drew a first figure from the housing-audit data, and this section takes the grammar further on the panel of the EU-frames case, read as `euframes <- readr::read_csv("data/EUframes_cy.csv")` in the workspace of that case. Its 270 rows are 27 countries in each of ten years, and its columns include the unemployment rate (`unemp`), the mean score of cosmopolitan framing of the EU among the respondents of each country-year (`mcosmo`, from 0 to 1) and whether an EU or IMF assistance programme was running (`bailout`), so it has the continuous measures that a scatterplot, a fitted line and a panel for each country need. Section 15 introduced the tidyverse as a family and named two of its members. **ggplot2** is the third, and it is the one that draws [@WickhamEtAl2019WelcomeTidyverse]. Almost every chart on the pages and slides of the course is built with it, so reading ggplot2 code is how you satisfy yourself that a figure shows what its caption says it shows. The figures that you draw yourself, in the workspaces and the browser labs, and the live class charts on the multiverse page of each case, are drawn with tinyplot ([section 12](#sec-tinyplot)), which is light enough to run in a browser. The other exceptions are the main chart of the [Multiverse page](../cases/eu-frames/multiverse.qmd) of the EU-frames case, which a script of the course draws in the browser, the charts of the [decision map](../cases/eu-frames/map.qmd), which Observable Plot draws, and a few figures in the methods modules that packages with plotting functions of their own draw.

The name abbreviates 'the grammar of graphics', the idea that any chart can be described as a combination of a few standard parts, much as a grammar describes how words combine into sentences. ggplot2 therefore has no separate function for each chart type. It splits a figure into parts that recombine freely: the data, the mapping from columns to visual properties, the geometric shapes drawn, the scales that decide what those shapes look like, the panels that the plot is divided into, and last the labels and the styling. A scatterplot and a bar chart are two fillings of the same slots, and once you know the slots you can read the figures on this site, including kinds you have not met yet.

### Data, mapping and geometry

A plot needs data, a mapping, and at least one geom. Everything else has a default good enough to start with.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point()
```

Three things happen there. `ggplot()` receives the data frame and declares which columns drive the picture. `aes()` is the **aesthetic mapping**, and it states that the unemployment rate governs horizontal position while the cosmopolitan-framing score governs vertical position. `geom_point()` adds a **geom**, a layer of geometric shapes, drawing one point per row – 270 points for 270 country-years. Axis ranges, tick marks, gridlines and the panel background are all inferred from the data, which is why this bare version is already a readable figure.

Layers are joined with `+`, never with the pipe `|>` of section 8. The reason is historical, since ggplot2 settled on `+` years before R had a native pipe. The practical consequence is that a long chain changes operator exactly once, at the point where it stops reshaping data and starts drawing, and typing `|>` where `+` belongs is among the commonest first-week errors in R.

### Mapping and setting

Every visual property of a layer can be given two ways, and confusing them is the next commonest error. Put a property inside `aes()` and it is **mapped**: its value is read from a column, it varies row by row, and ggplot2 adds a legend explaining the correspondence. Put the same property outside `aes()`, as an ordinary argument to the geom, and it is **set**, taking one fixed value for the whole layer, with no legend because there is nothing to explain.

```r
# MAPPED: colour comes from a column, so the points differ and a legend appears
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo, colour = factor(bailout))) +
  ggplot2::geom_point()

# SET: colour is a constant, identical for every point, and no legend appears
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(colour = "#0e3b6a", alpha = 0.5)
```

`alpha` controls opacity, running from 0 for invisible to 1 for solid, and setting it below 1 is the standard remedy for a scatterplot where points pile up on one another. The constant `"#0e3b6a"` is a hex colour code, the dark blue that the course figures use.

Leaving out the `factor()` wrapped around `bailout` produces the wrong figure without any warning. `bailout` is stored as 0 and 1 in numeric form, so `colour = bailout` gives ggplot2 a number, which it treats as continuous, drawing a colour gradient and a legend running smoothly from 0.00 to 1.00. What you wanted was two categories in two colours, and `factor(bailout)` is how you say so. The same applies to `year`, which is also numeric: map it raw for a gradient across the decade, or wrap it in `factor()` for ten discrete groups.

### Layers

A figure can have as many layers as you need, each with its own geom, and they are drawn in the order written, so later layers cover earlier ones.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#0e3b6a", fill = "#0e3b6a", alpha = 0.15)
```

The grey points are drawn first and the trend line over them. `geom_smooth()` fits a line through the cloud and draws it with a band showing the uncertainty around it, and `method = "lm"` asks for a straight line from the same least-squares method that the statistical methods module uses to fit models. R then prints the message `` `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x' ``, which only reports the relationship that was fitted and needs no action. Reference layers behave the same way: `geom_hline(yintercept = 0)` rules a horizontal line at zero, and section 17 uses one to split a figure into results that support a claim and results that do not.

Line thickness is set with `linewidth`, whereas point size and type size are set with `size`, and mixing the two up is behind a great many warnings.

```r
ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.4)   # the thickness of a drawn line
ggplot2::geom_point(size = 0.7)       # the area of a plotted point
ggplot2::geom_text(size = 3.5)        # the height of a piece of type
```

Passing `size` to a line geom still works, but R warns "Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0. Please use `linewidth` instead." The reason that the two names survive side by side is that `size` on a point means an area and on text a height, neither of which is a line thickness.

### Scales

The mapping says which column drives colour; the **scale** decides which colours it drives, and the same holds for positions, sizes and shapes. Every mapping gets a default scale, and you override it whenever the default is not what a reader needs.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo, colour = factor(bailout))) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(
    name   = "Assistance programme",
    values = c("0" = "#848c94", "1" = "#a10000"),
    labels = c("0" = "none", "1" = "bailout")
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 30, by = 5))
```

`scale_colour_manual()` names a colour for each level of the variable. Giving `values` and `labels` as *named* vectors, with `"0" = …` rather than a bare pair, means the assignment cannot silently reverse itself if the data ever arrives in a different order. The colours that the course uses throughout are `#0e3b6a` (dark blue), `#E69F00` (orange), `#009E73` (green), `#a10000` (dark red) and `#848c94` (mid grey), with `#c7ccd2` reserved as the muted grey for results that are not statistically significant. The orange and green belong to a palette built to stay distinguishable under the commonest forms of colour vision deficiency, which is why the decks never rest an argument on a red-green contrast alone.

Position scales follow the same override logic, and one of their arguments catches people out. `scale_x_continuous(breaks = …)` decides where the tick marks fall, but the sibling argument `limits` **removes** every row outside the range before any statistic is computed, so a smoother is refitted on whatever rows remain.

```r
p_trend <- ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#0e3b6a")

p_trend + ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.30, 0.50))   # drops rows, then refits
p_trend + ggplot2::coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.30, 0.50))        # keeps every row, only zooms
```

Run the first of those and R warns "Removed 163 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range (`stat_smooth()`)", and the trend line you are looking at now runs through 107 country-years rather than 270. `coord_cartesian()` zooms the finished figure instead and leaves the computation untouched, so it is the one to use when you only want a closer look.

### Facets

**Faceting** repeats the same plot once per group, on shared axes, so the groups can be compared by eye instead of by disentangling overlapping series. A country-year table suits it well, since each country can have a panel of its own.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = year, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ cntry, ncol = 6) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2004, 2008, 2013))
```

Twenty-seven small panels appear, one per country code, each showing the cosmopolitan-framing series of that country across the decade. The browser lab of the EU-frames case draws the same figure with tinyplot early in the exercise, so that the crisis years are in view before any model is fitted and it is plain how differently the countries move. The `~ cntry` is a one-sided formula, with nothing to the left of the `~`. The `lm()` call in section 18 uses the same syntax with an outcome written on the left. `ncol` fixes the shape of the grid. Where two grouping variables matter, `facet_grid(rows = vars(a), cols = vars(b))` crosses them into a matrix of panels.

### Labels and themes

Two layers finish a figure. `labs()` supplies the words – axis titles, plot title, subtitle, caption, legend name – and it deserves more care than beginners give it, because a column name such as `mcosmo` means nothing to a reader who has not opened the codebook. The **theme** then governs everything with no data behind it: type size, gridlines, background, the position of the legend.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = "#0e3b6a", fill = "#0e3b6a", alpha = 0.15) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x       = "Unemployment rate (%)",
    y       = "Cosmopolitan framing (mean score, 0–1)",
    title   = "Unemployment and cosmopolitan framing",
    caption = "270 country-years, EU-frames dataset"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    plot.title       = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position  = "top"
  )
```

`theme_minimal()` is the default look across the course, and `base_size` is its most useful argument, scaling every piece of type at once: 9 for a dense panel of small multiples, 12 for a page figure, 15 and upwards for a slide. A bare `theme()` afterwards overrides individual pieces, and the order matters, because a complete theme applied *after* your adjustments would wipe them out. Inside it, `element_blank()` deletes a piece outright, `element_text()` restyles type, and `element_line()` restyles rules and gridlines.

A plot is an ordinary R object, so you can store it under a name, extend it later, and write it to a file:

```r
p <- ggplot2::ggplot(euframes, ggplot2::aes(x = unemp, y = mcosmo)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Unemployment rate (%)", y = "Cosmopolitan framing")

p + ggplot2::geom_smooth(method = "lm") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggplot2::ggsave("figures/framing_unemployment.png", p, width = 7, height = 5, dpi = 300)
```

`ggsave()` takes its dimensions in inches and writes whichever format the file extension names. When you do not name a plot, it saves the last one drawn, which is convenient but can save the wrong figure, so name the object.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Draw the scatterplot of `unemp` against `mcosmo`, then change one thing at a time and watch what moves. Swap `geom_point()` for `geom_text(aes(label = cntry))` and each point becomes its country code; move `colour = factor(bailout)` from inside `aes()` to outside it and read the error it raises; drop the `factor()` and compare the two legends. Then add `facet_wrap(~ year)` and decide for yourself whether ten panels tell you more than one crowded cloud does.
:::

### From the pipe to the plot

Reshaping and drawing usually happen in one chain, with datawizard passing its result straight to ggplot2. The chain uses `|>` while it is still working on data and switches to `+` once `ggplot()` appears.

```r
euframes |>
  datawizard::data_filter(year >= 2009) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(mean_unemp = mean(unemp), by = "cntry") |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = reorder(cntry, mean_unemp), y = mean_unemp)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(fill = "#0e3b6a") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean unemployment, 2009–2013 (%)") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

`reorder()` sorts the country codes by the value being plotted rather than alphabetically, which turns a jumble of bars into a ranking you can read at a glance. `geom_col()` draws a bar whose height is the number stored in the data, which is what you want once `data_summary()` has already done the counting; its cousin `geom_bar()` counts the rows for you instead, and reaching for the wrong one of the two is a frequent small frustration.

Where two figures belong side by side, the **patchwork** package composes whole plots. `patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2)` sets two plot objects in a row, and `patchwork::wrap_plots(plots, nrow = 1)` does the same for a list of them; with the package attached by `library(patchwork)`, `p1 + p2` does it with the same `+` that adds layers.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Build a chain that keeps the crisis years, groups by `year`, and reports the mean of `mcosmo` and the mean of `mneg` per year, then pipe it into a plot with two `geom_line()` layers in different colours. You will find yourself wanting a legend and not getting one, because both colours were set rather than mapped. The remedy is to reshape the data into long form, with one row per year and outcome, using `data_to_long()` from datawizard (or `pivot_longer()` from tidyr), and then to map `colour` to the column that names the outcome.
:::

## 17. Reading the specification curve {#sec-speccurve}

The central figure of the course is a **specification curve**, and you now have every part needed to build one yourself. A hypothesis about a dataset admits many defensible analyses, and if you fit all of them and line the results up in order, you can see the range of answers that the data supports instead of the single answer that one analyst happened to report.

`data/spec_curve.csv` holds that curve for the EU-frames case: 864 rows, one per specification that the course judges a justifiable way of answering the claim, each recording the decisions that distinguish it from its neighbours, the partial correlation that it produced, and its p-values under several kinds of inference. The column `sig` records whether its p-value under standard errors clustered by country with the CR2 correction and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom lies below 0.05, the test that the course uses to class every point (the [statistics module](stats-methods.qmd#sec-inference) explains it), and `is_reference` marks the reference specification of the course, the analysis that analyst C6HJR submitted to Multi100, which is one of the three analyses that the one-day courses on the EU-frames case let you choose to reproduce in Task 3. Reading the file needs one preparatory step, which the paragraph after the code explains.

```r
curve <- readr::read_csv("data/spec_curve.csv") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(r_ca = dplyr::if_else(predictor == "growth", -r, r)) |>   # claim alignment
  datawizard::data_arrange("r_ca") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(rank = 1:n())

reference <- datawizard::data_filter(curve, is_reference)
```

The claim under test is that poor economic performance depresses the positive framing of the EU. With unemployment as the predictor, a negative correlation supports it, because a rise in unemployment is a worsening of the economy. With GDP growth as the predictor, support means a *positive* correlation instead, because a fall in growth is the worsening, and plotting the raw numbers together would scatter agreeing results on opposite sides of zero. **Claim alignment** repairs that. Flip the sign wherever the predictor is growth, and afterwards a negative value means support for every row alike. `if_else()` performs the flip, and the `_ca` suffix is the naming habit of the course for any claim-aligned quantity. The file already carries the aligned value in a column of the same name, so the line rebuilds something that you can check against the stored column. Sorting by the aligned value and numbering the rows then gives each specification a rank, and that rank becomes the horizontal axis.

```r
ggplot2::ggplot(curve, ggplot2::aes(x = rank, y = r_ca)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.4, colour = "#848c94") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(shape = sig), size = 1.1, alpha = 0.5, colour = "#0e3b6a") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = reference, colour = "#8b1538", size = 3) +
  ggplot2::annotate(
    "text",
    x = reference$rank, y = reference$r_ca - 0.08,
    label = "the reference specification\n(C6HJR, t = -3.804)",
    colour = "#8b1538", fontface = "bold", size = 3.2, hjust = 1
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(
    name   = NULL,
    values = c("TRUE" = 1, "FALSE" = 4),
    labels = c("TRUE" = "CR2 p < 0.05", "FALSE" = "CR2 p ≥ 0.05")
  ) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.65, 0.2)) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x     = "specification, ranked by claim-aligned partial correlation",
    y     = "claim-aligned partial correlation",
    title = "The curve of the claim"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

Almost everything in that block has come up already: a reference line, a layer of small points whose shape is mapped to a logical column, a second point layer drawn from a *different* data frame, a manual scale, a zoom, labels and a theme. The manual scale sets the convention of the charts of the course, an open circle for a result below the 5% threshold and a cross for one above it, drawn at the same size and in translucent ink so that dense stretches of the curve stay readable and the class of a point is read from its shape rather than from a colour. `data = reference` inside the geom overrides the frame given to `ggplot()`, and that is how a single row gets picked out and emphasised. `annotate()` is the one function you have not met. It adds a mark that comes from no column at all, since you supply the coordinates and the text yourself, and that is why its position is read off `reference` rather than mapped.

Every point below the grey line is an analysis in the direction of the claim. Of the 864 specifications, 98.1% lie below it and 77.2% lie below it with a CR2 p-value under 0.05. The aligned correlations run from −0.589 to 0.116, so the curve holds firm support and a few results on the other side of zero. The burgundy point is the reference specification, the analysis that C6HJR submitted to Multi100, with a t-statistic of −3.804. Of the other specifications, 583 lie further below zero than it does, and with a CR2 p-value of 0.050 it is drawn as a cross. The submitted analysis was neither an outlier nor a cherry-pick, and yet the same menu, worked through in good faith by any competent analyst, would have produced a great many other numbers, most of them further in the direction of the claim.

::: {.callout-tip}

Rebuild the curve, then add `colour = estimator` inside the `aes()` of the first point layer and delete the fixed `colour = "#0e3b6a"` that follows it, keeping the shapes as they are. ## 18. Naming the estimand {#sec-easystats}

Fitting models is the subject of the methods modules. On these data, the [binary-outcomes module](binary-outcomes.qmd) builds from the table of counts of section 10 up to the logistic regression of the paper. Nothing that follows is needed for the tasks. It is here because it completes the map of the dialects, and because it ties the tools of R to the habit that the course asks of you throughout, which is to name the quantity you want before you estimate it.

Take the simplest model of the claim, a linear model of the greeting on the group of the name, fitted to the replies that carry a greeting code. With an outcome of 0s and 1s and a predictor made of groups, each coefficient is a difference between two shares, the quantity of [section 10](#sec-shares). One step comes first. The modelbased package used below works through the marginaleffects package, which refuses a column called `group` because its own output has a column of that name, so the column is renamed, and made a factor with the white names first, before the model is fitted:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
replies <- audit |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(named)) |>
  datawizard::data_rename(select = "group", replacement = "names_of") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(names_of = factor(names_of, levels = c("white", "black", "hispanic")))

m <- lm(named ~ names_of, data = replies)
```
:::


In base R you call `summary(m)` and read the printout. The easystats packages instead give you one function for each question you might ask of the fitted model:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
parameters::model_parameters(m)     # the coefficient table as a data frame, with confidence intervals
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
(Intercept)         |        0.61 | 0.04 | [ 0.54,  0.68] |  16.39 | < .001
names of [black]    |       -0.05 | 0.05 | [-0.15,  0.05] |  -0.98 | 0.328 
names of [hispanic] |       -0.20 | 0.05 | [-0.30, -0.10] |  -3.85 | < .001
```


:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```

  using a Wald t-distribution approximation.
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
performance::model_performance(m)   # fit indices, R2, AIC and the like, in one row
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# Indices of model performance

AIC   |  AICc |   BIC |    R2 | R2 (adj.) |  RMSE | Sigma
---------------------------------------------------------
800.3 | 800.3 | 817.5 | 0.028 |     0.025 | 0.492 | 0.493
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

report::report(m)                   # the model written out in sentences
```
:::


`model_parameters()` returns the coefficients as a data frame that you can filter, join or plot [@LudeckeEtAl2020ExtractingComputingExploring]. The row `names of [hispanic]`, in which the function has written the name of the column in words, is the gap between the Hispanic and the white names, on the scale of a share rather than in percentage points. `check_model()` draws the standard diagnostic checks in one figure [@LudeckeEtAl2021PerformanceRPackage], and `report()` writes the results paragraph itself, with the numbers drawn live from the object. Its words are generic, though. It calls each coefficient an effect, a word that a comparison among replies earns only under the assumptions that the [audit-experiments module](experiments.qmd#sec-posttreatment) sets out, and a sentence written for any model needs editing before it describes this one. In a rendered Quarto document the numbers in such prose cannot fall out of step with the model, as a number pasted in by hand can.

One member of the family, `modelbased`, builds the habit of naming the quantity into its functions [@MakowskiEtAl2025ModelbasedRPackage]. The coefficients in a table are whatever quantities the parameterisation of the model happens to produce, so that a different reference group would give different coefficients from the same fit. These functions make you *name the quantity you want* – the **estimand** – and then compute that quantity from the model:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
modelbased::estimate_means(m, by = "names_of")             # the expected share greeted by name, for each group of names
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

----------------------------------------------
white    | 0.61 | 0.04 | [0.54, 0.68] |  16.39
black    | 0.56 | 0.04 | [0.49, 0.63] |  15.92
hispanic | 0.41 | 0.04 | [0.34, 0.48] |  11.41

Variable predicted: named
Predictors modulated: names_of
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
modelbased::estimate_contrasts(m, contrast = "names_of")   # the differences between those shares
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

Level1   | Level2 | Difference |   SE |         95% CI | t(555) |      p
------------------------------------------------------------------------
black    | white  |      -0.05 | 0.05 | [-0.15,  0.05] |  -0.98 |  0.328
hispanic | white  |      -0.20 | 0.05 | [-0.30, -0.10] |  -3.85 | < .001
hispanic | black  |      -0.15 | 0.05 | [-0.25, -0.05] |  -2.96 |  0.003

Predictors contrasted: names_of

```


:::

The expected outcome under each condition and the contrast between two conditions are each a quantity that you can state in words before touching the software, and the contrast of the Hispanic with the white names is the gap of section 10 once more. Under the bonnet these functions call the `marginaleffects` package, which does the job that Stata users will know from `margins`. The intervals above rest on the ordinary standard errors of a linear model, which assume that the outcome varies as much in every group. `try_spec()` uses HC2 standard errors, which allow the variance of a 0/1 outcome to differ from group to group, and `estimate_contrasts(m, contrast = "names_of", vcov = "HC2")` asks for them here. Saying what you want to estimate first, and only then deriving the analysis that estimates it, is what the course practises in Task 2, with the estimand statement and the causal graph, and again in Task 5, where you state your specification and the quantity that it estimates in the preregistration block of your report before running it.
